overview:
North America is the third-largest continent on Earth, extending entirely within the Northern Hemisphere and almost entirely within the Western Hemisphere. It is bounded by the Arctic Ocean to the north, the Atlantic Ocean to the east, the Pacific Ocean to the west, and is connected to South America by the Isthmus of Panama in the southeast. The continent encompasses a vast range of climates and landscapes, including Arctic tundra in the far north, expansive boreal forests, temperate grasslands, deserts, and tropical regions in Central America and the Caribbean.

Geographically, North America includes three large countries—Canada, the United States of America, and Mexico—along with the nations of Central America (such as Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Panama) and the island states and territories of the Caribbean (including Cuba, Jamaica, Haiti, the Dominican Republic, and many others). Major physical features include the Rocky Mountains, the Appalachian Mountains, the Great Plains, the Canadian Shield, the Mississippi–Missouri river system, the Great Lakes, and extensive coastal plains. These diverse environments support rich ecosystems and significant biodiversity, from polar bears and caribou in the north to tropical species in the rainforests and coral reefs of the south.

Historically, North America has been inhabited for tens of thousands of years by Indigenous peoples, including First Nations, Inuit, and Métis in Canada; Native American nations in the United States; and numerous Indigenous groups in Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean. These societies developed complex cultures, languages, and political structures, such as the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, the Maya civilization, and the Aztec Empire. European exploration and colonization began in the late 15th century, led primarily by Spain, France, and England, followed by other powers. Colonization brought profound changes: the displacement and decimation of Indigenous populations, the transatlantic slave trade, and the establishment of colonial economies and new political entities.

In the modern era, North America is a major center of global economic, political, and cultural influence. The United States and Canada are among the world’s largest economies, with advanced industrial, technological, and service sectors. Mexico and many Central American and Caribbean nations play crucial roles in regional trade, agriculture, manufacturing, tourism, and migration networks. Institutions such as the United States–Mexico–Canada Agreement (USMCA) and the Organization of American States (OAS) reflect efforts at economic integration and political cooperation.

Culturally, North America is characterized by significant diversity and ongoing interaction among Indigenous traditions, European settler cultures, African diasporic communities, and more recent immigrants from Asia, Latin America, and other regions. This diversity is expressed in languages, religions, arts, cuisines, and social movements. English, Spanish, and French are the most widely spoken colonial languages, alongside hundreds of Indigenous languages. Religious life includes Christianity in many forms, Judaism, Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism, Sikhism, and Indigenous spiritual traditions. North American cultural production—literature, film, music, digital media—has global reach, shaping and reflecting debates about identity, democracy, environment, and social justice.

North America faces significant contemporary challenges and opportunities. Environmental issues include climate change, melting Arctic ice, wildfires, hurricanes, biodiversity loss, and pollution, prompting cross-border cooperation on conservation and sustainable development. Social and political questions involve Indigenous rights and sovereignty, migration and border policies, racial and economic inequality, urbanization, and the governance of rapidly changing technologies. At the same time, the continent’s scientific institutions, educational systems, and civil society organizations contribute to global innovation and dialogue. As a geographic, historical, and cultural entity, North America continues to evolve, shaped by its deep Indigenous roots, colonial legacies, and ongoing efforts toward more inclusive and sustainable futures.

primary_sources.title: Not applicable to Jain primary canon
primary_sources.author: N/A
primary_sources.translation: There is no direct canonical Jain Prakrit or Sanskrit primary text specifically about the modern geographic entity called North America.
primary_sources.notes: Jain primary scriptures (such as the Āgamas in the Śvetāmbara tradition and texts like Ṣaṭkhaṅḍāgama in the Digambara tradition) focus on cosmology, ethics, karma theory, and spiritual practice rather than modern continental geography. Any discussion of North America in Jain contexts is typically found in modern community education, diaspora literature, or comparative ethics, not in the classical canon.

misconceptions.myth: North America consists only of the United States and Canada.
misconceptions.reality: North America includes Canada, the United States, and Mexico, as well as the countries of Central America (such as Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Panama) and the island nations and territories of the Caribbean. The continent is a broader geographic and political region than just its two largest northern countries.

misconceptions.myth: North America has a single, unified culture dominated only by English-speaking populations.
misconceptions.reality: North America is culturally diverse, with Indigenous nations, Spanish-, French-, and English-speaking communities, and large populations with roots in Africa, Asia, Latin America, and Europe. Hundreds of Indigenous languages and traditions coexist with multiple colonial and immigrant cultures, creating a complex mosaic rather than a single homogeneous culture.

misconceptions.myth: Indigenous peoples in North America largely disappeared after European colonization.
misconceptions.reality: Despite severe population loss, displacement, and systemic oppression, Indigenous peoples across North America continue to live, organize, and sustain their cultures, languages, and political structures. Many nations are actively engaged in cultural revitalization, legal struggles for land and sovereignty, and contemporary governance.

misconceptions.myth: North America is uniformly wealthy and developed.
misconceptions.reality: While parts of North America, especially some regions of the United States and Canada, are highly industrialized and economically powerful, the continent also includes areas facing significant poverty, inequality, and limited access to healthcare, education, and infrastructure. Economic and social conditions vary widely between and within countries.
